blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — adult weight-status screening and health-risk education
stem: An adult client’s BMI is 32 kg/m². Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.A: A BMI of 32 kg/m² is in the Class 1 obesity range; because BMI is a screening measure, it should be interpreted with other clinical factors when assessing health.
options.B: A BMI of 32 kg/m² is in the overweight range; the adult obesity category begins at 35 kg/m² unless additional metabolic risk factors are present.
options.C: A BMI of 32 kg/m² establishes the presence and severity of metabolic disease by itself, so other health information adds little to the assessment.
options.D: A BMI of 32 kg/m² is a healthy-weight value in a younger adult because adult BMI categories vary primarily with age and sex rather than fixed ranges.

rationale: CDC classifies adult BMI from 30.0 to less than 35.0 kg/m² as Class 1 obesity. CDC also states that BMI is a screening measure and should be considered with other factors when assessing an individual's health. Therefore A is correct. B is incorrect because 32 kg/m² is already within the Class 1 obesity range. C is incorrect because BMI does not independently establish metabolic disease or its severity. D is incorrect because for adults age 20 years and older, CDC BMI categories use the same BMI cut points regardless of age or sex.
educational_objective: Classify an adult BMI of 32 kg/m² as Class 1 obesity while recognizing that BMI is a screening measure that must be interpreted with other clinical information.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_version_date: Page dated March 19, 2024; live CDC page retrieved 2026-08-26
source_locator: At a glance; BMI categories for adults 20 and older; BMI is a screening measure: Class 1 obesity = 30 to <35 kg/m²; adult categories apply regardless of age or sex; BMI should be considered with other factors when assessing health.
source_claim_supported: For an adult, BMI 32 kg/m² is Class 1 obesity, and BMI is a screening measure rather than a stand-alone diagnosis of health or metabolic disease.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance — prevention, screening, health-maintenance recommendations and age-appropriate health education.
correction_summary: Rebuilt all options to remove the distractor-only absolute term and correct-answer length cue while preserving CDC's exact BMI category and screening limitation.

audit_findings.stem: PASS — specifies an adult and a single BMI value sufficient for CDC category classification without requiring unstated comorbidity information.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — exactly matches CDC Class 1 obesity range and the screening-measure limitation.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — plausible category-boundary error, but obesity begins at BMI 30, not 35.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — plausible overinterpretation, but CDC explicitly treats BMI as a screening measure considered with other health information.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — plausible age-related misconception, but adult BMI categories are not changed by age or sex.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only option that correctly gives both the BMI category and the proper interpretation of BMI's screening role.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B uses the wrong cutoff; C overstates diagnostic meaning; D contradicts the adult-category rule.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — option lengths and structures are balanced; no distractor-only absolute-word pattern remains.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — adult screening and health-risk interpretation fit Health Promotion and Maintenance.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether obesity terminology alone could overdiagnose disease. CDC explicitly labels 30 to <35 kg/m² as Class 1 obesity while also calling BMI a screening measure, so A preserves both facts and remains uniquely best.
